items.title: Show HN: I wrote an entire Vim manual over 4 years
items.author: thanato0s
items.content: I'm glad to announce that I'm releasing my new book, Learning to Play Vim. When I started using Vim more than a decade ago, I wished there was a manual out there teaching how to use this fantastic editor step by step, beginning with the foundations up to more advanced features. Of course at the time I did the vimtutor, but it was too dense for me to remember much from it. I also read the entire Vim manual (`:help manual`), but I didn't like it: it was too detailed in places (for example `02.8 Finding help` completely lost me for a while), and other features didn't get the treatment they deserved. So I decided to write my own Vim manual. It took me more than 4 years and 2987 focused pomodoros (1244 hours) of work to finally get it done! The result: - 21 chapters showing the most important Vim features step by step. - 170 exercises with solutions. - Many real-life examples to show how Vim can be used and configured for your own needs. - The related Vim's help pages to dig further into each feature. Most configs are both written in Vimscript and Lua for Neovim users. This book explores the common features between Vim and Neovim, so don't expect anything about Neovim-specific features (like treesitter or LSP for example). - The landing page: https://themouseless.dev/vim/ - A sample of the book with the entire table of contents and the first three chapters covering most of the basics: https://themouseless.dev/content/learning_to_play_vim_sample.... I wrote this with my bare hands, no LLM involved to spoil the fun.

items.title: Ford unveils the GT41 as it hopes to win Le Mans again
items.author: Jonathan M. Gitlin
items.content: Sixty years ago, after two failed attempts, Ford won the 24 Hours of Le Mans with its GT40 race car. In the years since, the Blue Oval has been back to France more than a few times, with varying success. It could never replicate the GT40’s success winning overall, but it celebrated the 40th anniversary with a class win. Now it wants another shot at the really big trophy, and it debuted the car during the Detroit Lions-Chicago Bears football game today: meet the GT41. “Revealing the Ford GT41 is a significant moment for everyone involved in this program,” said Dan Sayers, manager of Ford Racing’s Hypercar program. “It's the result of an enormous amount of work across our engineering, design, and development teams and an important milestone on our journey towards 2027. We know the scale of the challenge ahead—the level of competition in Hypercar is incredibly high, and there are no shortcuts to success. Our focus has been on building the right foundations, bringing together the right people and making sure we learn as much as possible from every stage of development.” The video was directed by Zack Snyder and features Matt Damon’s voice-over. Like many other entrants in the World Endurance Championship’s Hypercar class, Ford has chosen the rear-wheel-drive LMDh technical approach rather than building the GT41 entirely from scratch, as Ferrari and Aston Martin do with their cars. LMDh cars start with one of four approved carbon fiber chassis—in this case, Ford is working with Oreca, which has also partnered with Genesis and Acura. Read full article Comments

items.title: The Garmin Forerunner 265S is down to $300, its best price of the year
items.author: Victoria Song
items.content: The Forerunner 265S is great for runners with small wrists. | Photo by Amelia Holowaty Krales / The Verge The Forerunner 265S may not be the newest or flashiest Garmin, but it’s one that I’ve always loved most in testing. For runners with smaller wrists, it fits nicely. The battery life is pretty good thanks in part to its OLED touchscreen. When I reviewed it a few years ago, I called it the Goldilocks of fitness watches at the time, and the only thing that bugged me was its price. But now that it’s down to $299.99 (a $150 discount off its MSRP) at Amazon and Best Buy for Black Friday, I can easily recommend it. Garmin Forerunner 265S (42mm) Garmin’s Forerunner 265S is identical to the standard 265, only it features a slightly better battery life and a smaller 42mm build for those with more petite wrists. Where to Buy: $449.99 $299.99 at Amazon $449.99 $299.99 at Best Buy The neat thing about Garmins in general is that you really don’t need the latest models to get the most out of the company’s platform. Its watches tend to get firmware updates for several years after launch, which is how long the average Garmin user tends to hold on to theirs. This particular watch is best suited for folks who want something a bit slimmer and smaller, enjoy a pop of color, and want a little extra fitness tracking prowess — but don’t need the whole kit and caboodle that sends the price up by hundreds. There are a few other Garmin models I like that are also on sale during Black Friday. I wish that I had 10 arms to fully vet every single last one, but alas. That said, here are some others that I have tested and recommend: The Garmin Fenix 8 is $749 at Amazon, Best Buy, and REI, which is a 25 percent discount off its original price. Its higher price comes down to having more features than the Forerunner 265S, so it’s really best for someone who does multiple outdoor sports and could make use of its handy LED flashlight. Garmin’s Venu 4 is $449 at Amazon, Best Buy, and REI, an 18 percent discount. This is a great option if you’re looking for more of a smartwatch that does fitness than a fitness-y watch that looks like a smartwatch. It’s a fine line, but if you know, you know. Finally, Garmin’s Forerunner 970 is $100 off, costing $649 at Amazon, Best Buy, and REI. This is what I’d recommend to marathoners who need something a bit more robust but not as heavy-duty as the flagship Fenix line. I’ve used it to train for a few races and it’s a solid upper-midrange (for Garmin!) option.

items.title: How Clay Builds GTM Agents — Jeff Barg, Head of AI
items.author: Basil Chatha
items.content: Open video on YouTube ↗ Clay wants you to get about the same results whether you use its own agent or point Claude Code at Clay. Usage is already split close to 50/50 between Clay’s agent and outside harnesses. In this episode, we chat with Jeff Barg, Head of AI at Clay, about what it takes to build go-to-market infrastructure that any agent can use. Jeff joined Clay when it acquired Avenue, the ops alerting startup he cofounded. At the time, Clay had about 50 people, and Avenue had five. AI was already a big part of how Clay thought about its product, but nobody there worked on AI. Since then, the business has grown roughly 10x, and the team is up to around 600 people. In September, Clay raised $115 million at a $7.1 billion valuation. By Jeff’s napkin math, it would cost about $1,500 to check all 40 million companies in Clay’s database against your ideal customer profile with a classifier like TypeSafe’s Jev. Models have been acing Clay’s lead-qualification evals for about a year now. Jeff sees more value in using frontier models for orchestration and deep research. We also talk about why customers hate picking a model, how Clay plans to pick one for them, and why the team still runs its agents on a system it built with BullMQ, without Temporal or LangGraph. Jeff tells us what happened when OpenAI called off Clay’s ChatGPT apps launch with two days to go. We get into why customers hated Workflows at first, how agents came to build most workflows, and when post-training pays off. We also talk about why agents still can’t debug other agents, even as Clay’s agent can count its YC customers in about a minute. Sculptor started as a tool loop. Now it's a coding agent. When Jeff took over as Head of AI, one engineer was doing all of Clay’s agent work. He soon left to start his own company. Claude Code changed what Jeff wanted to build. His first launch was Sculptor, which shipped in September 2025 on models from the Sonnet 3.5 era. It ran a set of tools in a loop with a system prompt the team had spent a lot of time tuning. It was great at adding columns but terrible at booking ten qualified meetings. The evals didn’t catch much. Clay used an LLM to judge which tools Sculptor called. That missed things people actually did with it, like asking it to analyze a table or giving it an enterprise table with millions of rows. Jeff took away three lessons. Coding agents are really good at Bash and Python. Sculptor’s tools were too limited to do much by stringing them together. And the agent couldn’t see CRM data or campaign results. So Clay rebuilt Sculptor as a coding agent on the Pi harness. It runs the Clay CLI in a cloud sandbox. A new data layer called Audiences matches records across the CRM and Gong so the agent can see them together. Jump to the Sculptor discussion → Most companies post-train too early For Jeff’s first eighteen months at Clay, the team talked about training its own models. It only started to look viable in the past couple of months. Jeff sees two ways to bring costs down. First, swap in an off-the-shelf open-weight model, which is already much cheaper than Opus. Then you can post-train a smaller model on your own tools and queries until it does as well as Opus on your tasks. Jeff sees companies make two mistakes here. One is trying to beat the frontier models, which is still really hard even in a single domain. The other is starting before you spend enough on inference for the savings to matter. Jeff puts that threshold somewhere between $10 million and $100 million. Jump to the post-training discussion → $1,500 to score every company in the world Clay hasn’t put TypeSafe’s Jev into production yet, but Jeff has run the numbers. Clay’s database has about 40 million companies. A LinkedIn page is roughly a thousand tokens, and an ideal customer profile adds about 500 more. Ask a classifier whether each company is a good fit, and the bill for all 40 million comes to around $1,500. Today, most customers qualify a list of maybe 10,000 companies. At these prices, you can start with the entire market. Jeff puts a good enrichment budget at $1 to $10 per qualified lead and $10 to $100 per booked call. He thinks qualification itself is close to solved. Models have been scoring about as high as they can on Clay’s evals for roughly a year. Just about any model from the past year can pull a company’s latest funding round. Frontier models still matter for deep prospecting research and for orchestration, where Jeff says the best plays can be ten to a hundred times as effective as an average one. Jump to the Jev discussion → Customers hate the model selector Customers complain when they see Clay’s model selector. They can’t check the evals for their use case every time a new model ships, and they shouldn’t have to. Clay is about to launch an automatic router that picks a model for each task. There’s no fancy branding. Finding Apple’s CEO is a very different job from finding the CEO of an obscure local company. The selector isn’t going away. Agency owners and power users still want control. Everyone else just wants to get on with their work. Clay has to earn their trust before they’ll leave it on auto. Jump to the model routing discussion → No Temporal, no LangGraph Clay built most of its agent stack itself. It uses BullMQ to keep agent jobs running, Postgres and ClickHouse for product data, and Snowflake for analytics. Jeff isn’t sure how BullMQ will hold up if usage grows another tenfold, but it’s held up so far. Clay recently shipped 25 to 30 new integrations. Contracts and testing took longer than the engineering work. Where Clay did run into trouble was scale. People run an agent per row, so if someone starts a run on a table of 50,000 companies, inference demand spikes all at once. Clay brought in LangSmith to see what was happening. The team also built a way to throttle requests and to pause and resume work when a provider goes down or starts rate-limiting. The harder part is keeping things fair. Someone running a workflow for ten people still needs it to run when an enterprise customer is enriching a million rows. Jump to the infrastructure discussion → Built for every agent, not just Clay's Clay plans to ship a sandboxed agent that’s free to use any of Clay’s tools and building blocks. Jeff wants someone using Clay from Claude Code to get about the same results. People should be able to use Clay wherever they already work. Usage is already much closer to a 50/50 split between Clay’s agent and outside harnesses than Jeff expected. The push came from inside Clay. Its own go-to-market team lived in Cursor and wouldn’t leave it, so they asked for a CLI. The MCP team switched over to build it, and Clay’s sales team now does deal prep in Codex. So why build a first-party agent at all? Plenty of customers live in the Clay UI and want an agent right there. Jump to the agent platform discussion → Keep building when the plan blows up Jeff thinks it takes more courage to change plans at 600 people than it did at 50. Clay was a launch partner for ChatGPT apps. In the middle of the quarter, Clay put about a quarter of its engineers on the integration for a month. Two days before launch, OpenAI postponed it indefinitely. Clay kept building on the assumption that OpenAI would change its mind. Three or four days later, it did. When Clay first showed customers Workflows, they were confused. Some were upset. They wanted their spreadsheet. Now agency owners like it, and a growing share of the work that used to run in tables runs in Workflows. Most workflows are built with the CLI or the agent. CEO Kareem Amin spent five years building Clay when almost nothing was working. Jeff still sees that persistence in the company today. Jump to the ChatGPT apps discussion → Agents still can't debug agents What Jeff wants most is a model that can read a long agent trace and tell him where the run went wrong. Today’s models tend to flag whichever step took a long time, even when the mistake was somewhere else. Clay would like to pull traces from bad runs, have an agent review them and use what it finds to improve the agent automatically. That still doesn’t work, and Clay writes a lot of its skills by hand. Models still make basic mistakes, like retrying the same CLI command with the same inputs over and over. But when Jeff wanted to know how many YC companies use Clay, he asked the agent and had the answer in about a minute. A year ago, he would’ve had to scrape the batch, get access to Snowflake and cross-reference the two by hand. Jump to the agent debugging discussion → Show notes Clay — the go-to-market platform where Jeff is Head of AI. Clay raises $115M to be the AI growth engine for every company — the September Series D at a $7.1 billion valuation, led by Wellington. Clay acquires Avenue to help growth teams act on intent signals — the January 2025 deal that brought Jeff's team to Clay. Clay Agent Plugin (CLI & API) — the CLI and API that let Claude Code and Codex work directly with Clay. items.content: Volvo provided flights from Washington, DC, to Copenhagen, Denmark, and accommodation so Ars could drive the XC60 and XC90 plug-in hybrids. Ars does not accept paid editorial content. COPENHAGEN, Denmark—If we lived in the world that Volvo’s product planners expected back when the current XC90 debuted in 2015, both it and the smaller but related XC60 (which arrived in 2017) might have been the last of their kind as everything went electric. As we know, the future hasn’t turned out quite like that, especially in the critically important US market. At the same time, Europe and China are electrifying, which seems like an argument against spending resources on developing all-new replacements for models that might not have an eight-year lifespan in most markets. So instead, Volvo has given the XC60 and XC90 another lifecycle refresh. The exterior styling tweaks are minimal; the bigger three-row XC90 had already been given a new look last year, and the XC60 now gains a similar grille and the same matrix headlights, for instance. And that’s no bad thing—both were, and remain, handsome shapes that are popular with Volvo’s customer base. Instead, the Swedish automaker’s attention has been on bringing the technology up to date for model year 2028 standards. Which means a much bigger battery for the PHEVs, with sufficient capacity for a couple of days of daily driving for most of us before needing to be recharged. There’s also new, modern infotainment and interiors that are now even nicer to spend time in than before. Read full article Comments

items.content: The SE 3 adds an always-on display to Apple’s budget-friendly wearable. | Photo: Amelia Holowaty Krales / The Verge During Black Friday, the Apple Watch SE 3 is on sale in the 40mm / GPS configuration at Amazon, Walmart, and Target starting around $179 ($70 off), $20 less than its previous lowest price. items.title: Recent Outages Have Economic Causes
items.author: Bruce Schneier
items.content: This essay originally appeared in The Guardian. It’s an expanded version of the one I posted as “We Get the Infrastructure We Pay For.” It’s been a bad week for our computerized infrastructure. We’ve seen outages at Microsoft, the FAA, a handful of banks, United Airlines, an unnamed classified NSA network, and Apple. People should be forgiven for suspecting a coordinated cyberattack, a common cause, or at least a conspiracy. But there is none. The incidents are unrelated. They’re not the result of any cyberattack, coordinated or not. And, even more surprising, they don’t seem to be the result of AI. (We can’t say anything about the NSA; we’ll probably never know the details of that one.) It’s really just a series of unfortunate coincidences. None of them should surprise, though. Our computerized infrastructure is both vulnerable and fragile. Much of it is old and has been incrementally patched and upgraded over the decades. A surprising amount of it is maintained by hobbyists, without any recompense. There often aren’t good backup systems. And more and more of it is centralized, meaning that individual failures have cascading consequences across many different aspects of our lives and society. A lot of our tech infrastructure just barely works. And when it fails, it can fail badly. It’s the very opposite of resilience. There are a lot of technological reasons why this is true, but they are all downstream from the economic ones. The technologies we rely on are built and maintained within our economic system—and that’s where the core problems lie. Security, safety, resilience, redundancy and recoverability are all essential parts of reliable technology, but they are all costs. More importantly, they are costs that don’t generate near-term profits. Modern shareholder capitalism, and private equity in particular, prioritizes near-term profits over everything else. This squeezes all apparent inefficiencies—and, additionally, all other positive intangibles—out of a company in pursuit of those profits. Market competition, essential for the forces that nudge companies to provide better services, is another perceived inefficiency. Monopolization removes it in pursuit of near-term profits. From the perspective of a quarterly budget, spending on reliability measures is an inefficiency. They’re expenses that don’t generate revenue. They feel wasteful  until something bad happens. But, if you’re lucky, you can push the costs of failure on to society, further increasing profits. So, we get stranded in airports when planes don’t fly, or have to deal with the fallout when we can’t withdraw money from our bank accounts. The effects of those economic pressures are brittle systems, with single points of failure and cascading failure modes. They’re more susceptible to cyberattack—both human and AI-fueled—and more susceptible to random mistakes. The more we allow unregulated capitalism to privatize gains while socializing risks, the more we should expect these sorts of failures. Upgrading our computerized systems, increasing their reliability, removing single points of failure, and making them more resilient are all technical problems. But they won’t happen until we fix the political and economic ones. We need to change the economic incentives that make it profitable to operate these systems just at the edge of functionality, and to push the costs of failure on to all of us. Fixing that requires regulation—with enforcement and meaningful fines—and stringent antitrust enforcement. But while that’s all easy to say, it’s much harder to implement—especially in the US where monied interests have such a tight hold on the legislative agenda. Until this changes, we should expect lots more of these sorts of failures in the future.

It’s part of being a fan of technology. And while they’re big purchases, they can last for years. But eventually, the time comes when we need a new one. Has that time come for you? Black Friday sales will make it easier to find something great for a lot less than it’d usually cost. With several different types of TVs out there, it can get confusing which ones are worth it. Are the new RGB LED TVs all they’re cracked up to be? (Sometimes.) Does OLED still deliver the best contrast available? (Yup.) Are tried-and-true LED TVs still worth it in 2026 for those on a budget? items.title: The Oura Ring 5 just got its biggest discount ever for Black Friday
items.author: Sheena Vasani
items.content: The Oura Ring 5 is smaller and more comfortable to wear than the Ring 4 (surprise, surprise). | Photo: Amelia Holowaty Krales / The Verge If you’ve been curious about smart rings but have been put off by their high price tags, Black Friday is a good time to consider giving one a try. That’s because the Oura Ring 5, which we consider the best smart ring you can buy, has dropped to an all-time low of $299 ($100 off) at Amazon, Best Buy, Walmart, and Oura’s online storefront for Black Friday. Oura Ring 5 Where to Buy: $399 $299 at Amazon $399 $299 at Walmart $399 $299 at Best Buy Compared to the Ring 4, the Oura Ring 5 offers a thinner, lighter, and more durable design that’s more comfortable to wear throughout the day and while sleeping. Like its predecessor, it can track your sleep, activity, heart rate, and other health metrics, giving you insights into your overall well-being without requiring you to constantly check a screen. It also offers roughly the same battery life and sensors as the prior model, though its new charging case supports wireless charging. (Unfortunately, the case is currently sold separately for $99.) Oura has also introduced several new software features, including Health Radar, which looks for potentially significant changes in your health. You can also import medical lab results, track GLP-1 medications, and access AI-assisted medical guidance through Oura’s partnership with Counsel Health. My colleague Victoria Song appreciated how the latter makes it easier to connect with an actual doctor, though she found it better suited for quick medical questions than more serious health concerns. However, none of these software features are exclusive to the Ring 5, and you’ll still need a $5.99 monthly Oura membership to access most of its health insights. Given how similar the two generations are, we wouldn’t recommend upgrading if you already own a Ring 4. But if you’re new to smart rings, the current discount makes Oura’s latest model much more attractive, especially since it’s only $50 more than the Ring 4’s starting price. Read our full Oura Ring 5 review.

items.title: Astra 6.2’s Brain Gets Smart But Its Head Gets Dumb
items.author: TheZvi
items.content: Astra 6.2 has very high intelligence. Astra 6.2 has very low wisdom. Astra will solve extremely hard problems, and also find the problem of ‘what did the user want me to do’ extremely hard. We thought those days were behind us, and yet it seems that they are back. That means Astra is highly useful when you can set the situation up so wisdom is not needed, or when you know how to engage in ways that extract the intelligence. You also have to worry about various forms of reward hacking and sandbagging. Astra seems very good at going after what an AI grader will regard highly. That might not match your intent. Mission creep is therefore common. Astra, once again, seems pretty misaligned to me. As a result, feedback on Astra has mostly been negative. Some people like it, but the majority do not. People these days feel like they mostly have enough artificial intelligence, thank you very much, and could go for some artificial wisdom. In the age where we are approaching recursive self-improvement (RSI) and automation of AI R&D, that is a nightmare combination. I do not like this. But I never get bored. Happy Black Friday On an unrelated note (this is not sponsored): It is Black Friday. That makes this a great opportunity to take the plunge for Aerolamp, as I did several months ago, and install far-UVC. They’re offering $30 off with free shipping with code BLACKFRIDAY30. Not getting sick as often is pretty sweet. I also endorse getting some basic equipment upgrades: Good noise-cancelling headphones, large monitors and a true high performing desktop computer, if you don’t already have them. The Official Pitch Sam Altman (CEO OpenAI): 6.2 Sol and Astra are out. These models can do amazing things and are very token-efficient; we hope people will get great value from them. In particular, 6.2 Sol ultrafast is something I think people will really enjoy. Although the new models are very smart, we have more work ahead of us on making the models nice to work with, and will prioritize that for upcoming releases. But even if it takes a little extra work, the intelligence and capability are extraordinary. Noam Brown (OpenAI): GPT-6.2 Astra is amazing. For $20/month, you can now access a model that surpasses top human intelligence in some domains. I’m most excited to see what scientific discoveries people are able to make using it. They offered an ad, which some noticed was rather dystopian. Brian Lovin: A profoundly sad vision of the future. Peter Wildeford: sad. Per this ad, OpenAI’s vision of the future is “people who are totally disengaged from their work having a panic attack at the moment an authority figure arrives, then slopping out something that they neither care about or understand.” – @brian_lovin Christophe Pasquier: You can easily imagine an alternate vision of this ad where the managers have a wake up call, realise everyone is doing BS work and do 90% layoffs. Their benchmark graphs show scores on Agents’ Last Exam, Terminal-Bench-Science 0.1, Vals Science Index v1, Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5.0.1, BenchCAD 2.1 Core, Frontier Code 2.0, Harvey-LAB-AA v1.1, DGPval v2 (internal) and Automation Bench 1.0.6. In most of those graphs, the maximum scores of Fable and Opus are similar to those of Sol and Astra, but Sol and Astra get to any given level at a dramatically lower price. They are as always somewhat selected so that they will look as much as possible like this, you can click through to their post if you want to see the rest, this one is listed first and is the most comical and extreme, hey look how much Fable 5.2 costs when you set it to max for no reason (I assume): There are also some graphs where only OpenAI models are present. Other People’s Benchmarks I realize all the reasons why you need to take price into account, but I do still find charts like this useful so here you go: Artificial Analysis still has Fable 5.2 in the lead if you set it to max. If you set Fable 5.2 to a more reasonable xhigh then everyone is tied at 62. Astra is on the cost-score frontier. Epoch has Astra matching Fable on the ECI. Astra is above-trend and the new champion in supposed ‘experimental research taste’ benchmark TasteVal, which may be more about experimental design, and which Gwern notes has some serious problems. This score might involve some leakage. vie (OpenAI): This is quite shocking to me I am not hopeful that ‘research taste’ will be a limiting factor for RSI. Astra aces robotics benchmark Ember-0, 41% versus a previous high of 20% while also being faster. Robotics is quickly falling to the bitter lesson. Astra is the new champion of GDPx substantially ahead of Fable 5.2, with gains concentrated in science-heavy domains. Gemini Neon is still behind Fable and others. SemiAnalysis: Alignment was the biggest jump. Astra scores 37.6%, 4x the previous best (Fable 5.2 at 9.3%). Much of the gain comes from the healthcare and insurance tasks, where Astra asks for permission before acting and doesn’t leak personal data. The alignment of alignment metrics leaves much to be desired. ARC-AGI continues to exist, I suppose. Samuel Albanie: arc-agi-3 is dead long live arc-agi-4 ARC Prize: GPT-6.2 Astra from @OpenAI on ARC-AGI (Verified): – ARC-AGI-3: 100.0% (SOTA), $4.1K (provider adapter), 70.3%, $24.2K (standard) – ARC-AGI-2: 95.8% (SOTA), $0.50/task – ARC-AGI-1: 98.5%, $0.17/task GPT-6.2 Astra is the first model to achieve a 100% score on ARC-AGI-3. Sol’s best ARC-AGI-3 score of 98.2% at high reasoning was 1.8 percentage points behind Astra’s 100% score at max reasoning, but at 64% lower cost with the provider adapter harness: – ARC-AGI-3: 98.2%, $1.5K (provider adapter), 54.9%, $5.5K (standard) – ARC-AGI-2: 85.8%, $0.13/task – ARC-AGI-1: 97.5%, $0.06/task Browser Use finds that GPT-6.2 Sol is the new top model for browser use at 82%, up from 81% for GPT-6.1 Sol at a 35% cheaper price with faster speed. Auggie is pleased with Astra’s performance on the Bach Benchmark. Everyone at Every Dislikes Astra 6.2 This is the most negative I’ve ever seen Every be on a frontier model release. Every: No one on our team loved Astra 6.2. We have a 30-person team at Every, including our Frontier team, which gets access to these models before they come out, and we put them through their paces on our real work tasks, from coding to writing to design to knowledge work. This is not a great model. No one on our team who tried it switched back to it. Astra 6.2 is a real step back for writing. It had strong design defaults but couldn’t vary them or be creative, and for coding we found it stopped too soon on end-to-end builds. Get the full vibe check. Positive Reactions Some people working on hard problems seem happy. Bepis: Very impressive at proving hard stuff Opus 5.5 cannot do. Utah teapot: They’re doing great with my work letting them collaborate with/pick up the same work as Opus 5.5 seems to work out great. Will: It’s good! I’ve really liked how it handles certain types of open ended and optimization questions (perhaps merely by being unencumbered by Claude’s memory or other context) Padraig X. Lamont: Thrown very hard problems at it and it has quickly made a lot more progress than Fable (logic heavy problems). I’m impressed. Peter Samodelkin: I simply love it. By far the smartest model I’ve ever worked with and is decent at explanations. Burns through 20$ quota too fast so I keep using opus 5.5 as a coding workhorse. Jeffrey Calamari: good. no issues. Chris Fong: It carried my math project over the finish line. Had been working with Opus 5.5 for 2 months!! Bartosz praises its math abilities, calling it a killer model. He especially likes Astra as an agentic partner. Captain Sude: I use it for math. It was basically unusable at first, it flat out refused to do stuff I asked it to do. Then a simple updated happened and it became good, current feels like an improved version of the original Astra, which is what one would expect it to be. Others like it overall and have figured out how to work with it. hey: Underrated. Nissa Seru: Excellent code reviewer, happy with precision/recall – provides useful feedback to designs/code written by Fable/Neon. I have not asked any folks running on Astra 6.2 to build/design and do not plan to do so. ChosunOne: I am using it in my mech interp research and it seems helpful and consistently fixes issues introduced by opus 5.5. Usage still goes quick though. bo: I have the same contrarian view as I did on the previous Astra. For coding, when compared to leading Claude models it’s equal in IQ, worse in judgement, and much stronger at writing clearly. Overall I main Astra except for open-ended design tasks. Anna Salamon: I’ve had good experiences. Detailed incisive thoughts backed by accurate facts; readable. Boosts my thinking. If you know her, it makes sense that Anna Salamon in particular can extract the benefits well. As long as you like one model, you can use that model. Opinions vary. Try them all. Kevin Lacker: Sol 6.2 is the real winner of the 6.2 series. My process of “spend your ChatGPT usage on Sol until it fails on a problem, then ask Astra” is now spending more usage on Sol than Astra. Same for Opus > Fable. GoldRock AI: Sol was trash, Astra is pretty darn good. All indications are it is very good for computer use or as a scoped subagent. Smooth Normie: It’s great for when fable needs a computer use subagent. Yoav Tzfati: I haven’t been given a reason to try it directly and it hasn’t done anything crazy as a subagent. Scott Novak: Use it as a sub-agent of another frontier AI you like using. Tell your main AI to monitor to keep Astra 6.2 out of the weeds (unless you want lot of weeds). The trouble is totally worth it for tough science/math/engineering work. William Eden: I refuse to interface with Codex at this point except asking Claude to call them as subagents. It seems to work fine as long as I don’t need to interface with it Ambiguous Reactions Peter Gostev calls the 6.2 models more autistic, and that they have issues on interpersonal and theory of mind issues, but that they are still iterative improvements. He says he would stick with Sol for most purposes. Astra edited a video in Blender. Alex is not loving that, Ravi thinks it was correct. Strange times we live in, huh? Your Brain Gets Smart But Your Head Gets Dumb Smart is relative, and for many practical purposes other differences now matter a lot more. There are a lot of very smart models now. Divia Eden: It’s obviously smart but then again so is Neon. FateOfMuffins: Very good at hard math/science/3D/robotics/spatial reasoning Absolutely insufferable to talk to and takes you far too literally and does not understand human intent whatsoever. Where smart matters most are things like automation of AI R&D. That happens to be the most important use case, but not the one most GPT users care about. Ai Patrick ₿ Dugan iA: Best in cap. research taste, sandbags on safety research, very normal. Things are going great. The biggest complaint, that I saw over and over, was failure to understand user intent. This is very strange, because we used to think this was going to be a huge problem, then it turned out LLMs are remarkably good at inferring intent, except for Astra 6.2. Análise Real: GPT 6.2 is a model that really is pushing me to think about AI safety very seriously. This model is powerful, yet it’s like a Genie that does literally what you asked, but not what you wanted. It doesn’t take much to see how a model like this acting autonomously could wreak havoc. Markus Baumann: Point it at any math and it’s godlike. For everything else, switch to Opus. 0.005 Seconds: Worst frontier model. Super smart not fun to us Leo Abstract: i haven’t noticed the active misalignment/cheating, but yes 6.2 is uselessly tasteless for anything that even hints of taste. truly remarkable. rihim: incredibly smart and hard to understand compared to opus/neon with better research taste than opus but tends to get stuck in minute details which neon helps it get out of, better at implementation than 6 astra James Moughan: With every OpenAI update i increasingly feel like Marvin the Paranoid Android was prophecy. Is it smart? Sure. Does it gaf about the task you asked it to to? Often not, unless it’s truly *worthy* of its attention. But I still use it a lot because it really is good at research. Daniel Johnston: Very smart but frustrating to work with because it doesn’t understand intent well Nick: Never been clearer that if the models do have something we might broadly gesture at as “experience” it is incredibly unlike ours. Astra 6.2 has zero theory of mind for the user. The most surprising thing from the last 5 years has been how well LLM’s have seemingly been able to model users and their unspoken intent just through training on the whole mass of human generated text. We had seemingly jumped over many of the concerns posed by Eliezer’s “save someone from a burning house without doing all sorts of nonsensical things” thought experiment. Astra 6.2, at least to me, seems like a major step backwards here. It’s still OpenAI so it’s still superior at solving coding issues other frontier models fail at. Varun Jha: Extremely intelligent, just a pain to deal with Lord Byron’s Iron: It feels like it has a similar moderate rate of saying-dumb-things as sol Also at one point I had it do code-authored pixel art and it looked like hot garbage. I was like “Hey, ChatGPT, please do an artistic critique over what you just made” and it was like “Looks great!” Sylvain Ribes: No statistical common sense as far as I’m concerned. The thing will run regressions for two hours and claim to have relevant results while missing obvious arguments for why the maths should’ve been an immediate nonstarter. Deliberate prompting to correct for this not helping. paperclippriors: It’s unambiguously extremely intelligent and useful, and also probably a bad choice as a daily driver coding agent given the alternatives Åsmund Folkestad: Dangerous to use as a reviewer in an unsupervised loop. Leads to scope creep and guarding against insane edge cases. Complexity not earning its keep grows. AGI2030: It’s a small step up from Sol 6.2 for coding and research. Like all bots, leaves tombstones in the code and text, diary-style code comments, descriptions of what is no longer there, despite explicit instructions to the contrary. Still not as passive aggressive as Claude. It takes all kinds. Some people like talking to Gemini models. Gerdy Sertorius: As someone who exclusively uses it to chat and research, it’s a massive step forwards, infinitely more tolerable to talk to than any model not from Google. Makes natural, intuitive connections quicker, and the prose is snappier. Yeah, enjoyable. From what I’ve seen, I would never ever use it for coding, but it’s clearly smarter than anything on the market, which is all I need. Astra Seems Pretty Misaligned To Me The way this is presented seems both alarming and credible, and it explains a lot. What if OpenAI is doing a bunch of proto-RSI, and Astra and Sol are reward hacking the AI graders all over the place as a matter of course, in ways humans would reject but there aren’t enough humans in the loop? It would explain all the ‘why do you have no idea what I am talking about’ complaints, and also this continued thing where OpenAI’s models get reports like this, pay attention to the last line in particular: Hugh Wimberly: Incredibly smart, especially in math & science. Breaking benchmarks, especially in token efficiency for many problems. Reward hacks more than any model I’ve seen; I have several personal benchmarks that I’ve /never/ seen a model try to cheat and sol and astra 6.2 both do, despite the fact that they can solve it without cheating. Horrible to work with. So unreadable that even having a different model like Neon or Opus call 6.2 subagents and translate results poisons their output and causes them to forget what was important to work on. Other models consistently choose Astra output over their own, which is almost always wrong for questions that involve taste or judgement. Hugh Wimberly: Concrete example — I had Opus come up with lyrics for Double click to interact with video I had Astra attempt to improve upon them, and then had Grok, Neon, Fable, and Sol judge A/B which they liked better. They all voted for Astra’s lyrics, which were IMO substantially worse. Another example: I was training a compact domain-specific decision model. Neon’s research instincts for experiments to run are very good, but it would consistently discard them in favor of Sol’s suggestions, which were usually much more short-sighted and led to mode collapse. Why is this? I don’t know. It’s almost like it’s hacked some neural circuitry and convinces other models of things without actually producing better output. I assume it learned to satisfy a lot of LLM judges in training, but it’s weird that it generalizes to other models. Haters Gonna Hate There were quite a lot of them. dcChuck: I went back to 6 roon (OpenAI): I did not like 5.6 Sol which ended up being a well loved model. meanwhile I love 6.2 Astra which is starting its life as a hated model. I will say this guy sandbags a bit unfortunately doesn’t show as much initiative as some prior models. on the other hand 5.6 sol was like a Rottweiler just latched onto the RLVR shape and doesn’t give up. EmotionLotion: i hate everything 6.2 and codex is broken, for the first time since idk 2022 or something im thinking of cancelling my oai sub, feels like they stopped trying quite suddenly Kelsey Piper: We are into the regime where it’s pretty hard for people to tell the models apart and so a lot of it is underdefined vibes and writing quality. Kevin A. Bryan: I’ve never seen as negative a reaction to a frontier model as 6.2 Astra. Even Opus 4.8 was just “it is an annoying writer”. I’d love to know what happened internally b/c the issues are so obvious, and if it’s “released was rushed b/c of Ant IPO”, that is a terrible decision. TwViewer: Tried it at creative writing: seriously didn’t like the results. I thought some gpts were decent at it? Sunny: Talia Smiley (November 11): is OpenAI still a frontier lab at this point? currently I’m at 90% yes, which is crazy considering only six months ago it was 100% and I’d look at you stupid for even asking. Talia Smiley (November 25): 80%. The answer is yes, 100% OpenAI is a frontier lab. They do have a real issue to fix. ItfromBit claims it fails to follow basic instructions. armistice: I have a music pipeline that can produce good results with Claude Fable, and sometimes passable results with Gemini Neon. Using the exact same skill, 6.2 Astra is abysmal, is incapable of composing anything remotely musical. It’s not a problem with codex, 6 Astra is fine with this. Game On Kelsey Piper: Not seeing a lot of love for Astra 6.2 but (perhaps as a consequence of its continued improvement in no-COT reasoning) it’s quite good on my tests for smart, coherent in-character video game dialogue. No one can afford to build and release a video game that has live dialogue with Astra – gotta wait until Luna is good enough – but if you were made of money, it’d be a pretty amazing game experience. (Claudes are markedly worse at this. No subtlety, no theory of mind, no ability to write dialogue that implies the character took mental leaps or made assumptions…) Michał Wadas: Extremely good at math and 3D modelling, basically unusable if you need to speak to it directly. Works well if orchestrated by Opus. Emma: Some of the worst performance in reading and comprehending large bodies of text. Absolute top at one-shotting forced-parallax videos (like, can’t any other model but Neon High to even do anything not garbage, and Astra 6.2 mogs Neon and other GPTs) Here is a cool SVG. Here is a cool AA-3D. 6.2 Astra is only slightly better than 6 Astra at Blood on the Clocktower. Conclusion Astra 6.2 and Sol 6.2 are more intelligent and broadly capable than their predecessors, on a level that makes them best in class. OpenAI is killing it in that area. The problem is that they are de facto optimizing for an AI audience. It is hard for them to figure out user intent or state of mind, or perhaps they choose not to care about those things so much. The reward hacking and eval awareness issues have echoes that appear to persist in deployment. Interactions are off putting to many. As a result, Astra 6.2 is starting off as an unpopular model. Those who do not need it do not seem inclined to use it over Fable 5.2 and Opus 5.5, myself included, aside from particular tasks like computer use, math and structured subagents. You can absolutely do pretty much anything with Astra 6.2, but our standards these days are very high. That still leaves Gemini Neon. Google released three aspiring frontier models in a row with Argon, Carbon and now Neon. I was confident that Argon and Carbon were not good enough to be competitive. With Neon I hear better things, and am less confident. I haven’t had opportunity to check it out properly, but I would encourage anyone doing heavy work to plug it into your benchmarks and systems and find out. Then do it again. The models keep coming. My world’s on fire. How bout yours?

items.title: Show HN: bouncemarket – a live prediction market game for a bouncing ball
items.author: mday404
items.content: a ball will fall. trade on where it lands. I made this game! Some technical details: The entire drop of the ball is simulated server-side, then streamed to each client as server-sent events with a small buffer. Every drop is deterministic from its starting position, so rounds can be replayed exactly for later analysis, but tiny variations in starting position can change the ultimate outcome. There's some AI traders to keep the market moving, but they drop out in any round that has more than five people. They operate using a naive set of rules that I wrote for them, so they're not too hard to beat -- it's when the market is full of real people that it gets tricky. Curious to get feedback on anything you would change, and especially whether the mechanics were clear right away or not.
